name: Cortisone injections for keloids
lead: Intralesional corticosteroid injection, commonly with triamcinolone acetonide, is a clinician-administered treatment in which a corticosteroid is injected directly into a keloid, a raised scar that grows beyond the original wound. It is used to flatten, soften and reduce the itch of keloids such as those on earlobes, chest and shoulders, so the scar becomes less prominent. Wikipedia reports that intralesional corticosteroids were introduced in the mid-1960s and are said to reduce fibroblast activity, inflammation and itching [1].

Keloids are most common in people of sub-Saharan African, Asian or Latin American ancestry, often appear between ages 10 and 20, and frequently follow piercing, particularly of the earlobes [1]. Wikipedia describes corticosteroid injection as one of several options, sometimes combined with 5-fluorouracil and pulsed dye laser in adults [1].

Registered clinical trials continue to compare steroid injection with other agents, including 5-fluorouracil, metformin, botulinum toxin and laser-assisted delivery. A published case report documents a reaction after an injection of triamcinolone with lidocaine [2].

paras: Keloids are fibrotic scars made of atypical fibroblasts that deposit excess collagen and other matrix, with thick collagen bundles forming nodules in the deep dermis [1]. They can follow piercing, burns, acne, surgery or vaccination, and sometimes appear without obvious injury [1]. Wikipedia says keloid scarring is common between ages 10 and 20 and occurs in roughly 15 to 20 percent of people of sub-Saharan African, Asian or Latino ancestry; about one-third of people with keloids have an affected first-degree relative, and a susceptibility region has been reported on chromosome 15 [1].

The name comes from the Greek for crab pincers, and 19th-century writers called the condition the keloid of Alibert [1]. Pressure therapy came into use in the 1970s and silicone gel sheeting in the early 1980s, after steroid injection in the mid-1960s [1].

Steroid injections are used to flatten and soften keloids and reduce itching. Wikipedia lists them alongside surgery, radiation, cryotherapy, pressure therapy and silicone sheeting, noting that surgical excision alone has a recurrence rate of 70 to 100 percent and that combining it with other therapies lowers recurrence [1]. Steroid injection after excision is itself studied, as covered in the keloid surgery and radiation entry.

A 2010 review of scar management reported good evidence supporting silicone sheets, pulsed dye laser, intralesional triamcinolone and dermabrasion in reducing hypertrophic scars, while noting that each needs qualifying by timing and scar type, and that raised areas injected with triamcinolone should be re-evaluated after about six weeks [9]. Wikipedia also describes adult triple therapy with corticosteroids, 5-fluorouracil and pulsed dye laser as improving results, and says radiotherapy, antimetabolites and corticosteroids should generally be avoided in children because of growth-related side effects [1].

A 2001 French case report described a patient who experienced fear of dying after an intra-keloid injection of triamcinolone acetonide with lidocaine, a reaction labelled Hoigne's syndrome [2]. Systematic adverse-event rates have not been reported.
Wikipedia's keloid article, which covers steroid injection among several options, does not give adverse event rates [1].

Registered trials include intralesional treatment of keloids in a 45-person phase 3 study that began in December 2024 and is recruiting [3]; triamcinolone versus triamcinolone with fluorouracil after surgery (7 participants, completed) [4]; intralesional metformin versus triamcinolone (30 participants, phase 2, completed) [5]; steroid injection alone versus combined with Nd:YAG or erbium laser (20 participants, completed) [6]; fractional ablation-assisted triamcinolone delivery (25 participants) [7]; and botulinum toxin to prevent recurrence (28 participants, phase 4, completed) [8]. Registry records reviewed list no outcomes, so effect sizes are not given here.

Published randomized trials have compared triamcinolone with add-ons. A trial of keloids after surgical incision compared triamcinolone alone with a triamcinolone-verapamil blend, treating until the keloids were nearly flat or for a maximum of eight sessions [10]. A study of 60 patients with refractory keloids compared triamcinolone alone with triamcinolone plus platelet-rich plasma [11]. A randomized controlled trial compared an intralesional triple combination with triamcinolone alone [12], and a randomized trial in transgender men with postmastectomy scars compared 595-nm pulsed dye laser plus intralesional corticosteroids with corticosteroids alone [13]. Outcome figures for these trials are not summarized here.

Keloids come up in appearance communities in discussions of piercing, acne and scar care, where people ask what a dermatologist can do for a raised scar. Wikipedia notes that tea tree oil, salt and other topical oils have no effect on keloids [1].

card.summary: A clinic-administered steroid injection into keloids, a long-standing option now being compared with newer agents in small trials.
card.note: Prescription clinical procedure; case reports describe reactions, and no outcomes from the listed trials were reviewed.

quick.overview:
A corticosteroid, usually triamcinolone, is injected into a keloid by a clinician to reduce inflammation, itching and fibroblast activity. Wikipedia lists it among standard keloid options.
Current registered trials compare it with fluorouracil, metformin, lasers and botulinum toxin.
quick.mechanism: Corticosteroids are described as reducing fibroblast activity and inflammation in the scar.
quick.risks: A case report describes a reaction after injection with lidocaine. Systematic adverse-event data are lacking.

chain: Raised scar flattens and softens, making it less visible
angle.text: Keloids can cause pain, itching and disfigurement [1]. Injections are one of the main medical ways of reducing their height and bulk, and they are often combined with other treatments in the clinic [1][3].
